subsystems.name: Input encoding
subsystems.role: turns the classical vector b and matrix A into quantum states.

subsystems.name: Hamiltonian simulation
subsystems.role: implements the time evolution e^(−iAt) that phase estimation relies on, using a sparse-matrix decomposition (e.g. Lie–Trotter or qubitisation).

subsystems.name: Phase estimation
subsystems.role: writes the eigenvalues of A into a register with enough bits to resolve them.

subsystems.name: Reciprocal rotation
subsystems.role: rotates an ancilla qubit by an angle proportional to 1/λ, inverting each eigenvalue.

subsystems.name: Uncompute and postselect
subsystems.role: undoes phase estimation and keeps only runs where the ancilla was measured in the right state.

subsystems.name: Readout
subsystems.role: extracts useful information from the solution state, usually by sampling observables rather than reading amplitudes.

buildSteps.title: Map the problem
buildSteps.detail: Write A as a sparse Hermitian matrix and b as a normalised vector, and check the condition number κ — runtime grows roughly linearly with κ.

buildSteps.title: Prepare b
buildSteps.detail: Load the vector's amplitudes into the system register, a step whose cost can wipe out the speedup unless b has special structure.

buildSteps.title: Evolve under A
buildSteps.detail: Run Hamiltonian simulation to apply e^(−iAt) for the time needed to resolve eigenvalues.

buildSteps.title: Estimate eigenvalues
buildSteps.detail: Phase estimation writes each λ into an ancilla register as a binary fraction; the register needs about log(κ/ε) bits.

buildSteps.title: Invert and rotate
buildSteps.detail: A controlled rotation maps λ to an ancilla amplitude of roughly C/λ, inverting small eigenvalues most strongly.

buildSteps.title: Uncompute
buildSteps.detail: Reverse phase estimation so the eigenvalue register returns to its initial state and the solution stays in the system register.

buildSteps.title: Postselect
buildSteps.detail: Measure the ancilla; keep only the successful outcomes, which occur with probability around 1/κ², and repeat until enough samples accumulate.

buildSteps.title: Read out
buildSteps.detail: Use the state as input to further quantum routines, or measure chosen observables many times to estimate output properties.

prerequisites.tech: Fault-tolerant quantum computer with thousands of logical qubits
prerequisites.why: HHL needs deep circuits and error correction; today's noisy machines cannot run it at useful size.
algorithms exist and small instances have run, but cost at practical matrix sizes is not demonstrated.
loading arbitrary classical data can cost more than the classical solve it replaces.
amplitudes cannot be read directly; only sampled properties are accessible, which limits which problems benefit.
the algorithm's advantage requires sparse, low-condition-number matrices and the right output model.

pathway.milestone: proof-of-principle runs on a handful of qubits solving tiny 2×2 or 4×4 systems
pathway.unlocks: confidence that the circuit blocks work, but no practical speedup.

pathway.milestone: early fault-tolerant versions that avoid full phase estimation and use error mitigation
pathway.unlocks: larger systems and cheaper circuits, still short of a proven advantage.

pathway.milestone: resource estimates for real problems (fluids, materials, machine learning) identifying where an advantage survives end-to-end costs
pathway.unlocks: a clear list of target applications worth chasing.

pathway.milestone: fault-tolerant demonstration on a problem where the whole pipeline beats the best classical solver on time or energy
pathway.unlocks: a genuine quantum linear-solver tool, and a template for other algorithms.
